intro: Elgar’s hesitant G-minor theme flowers into a portrait of his wife, Alice, without a break. The Hallé and John Barbirolli play the opening pair of his Enigma Variations.

sections.label: Theme · Strings in G minor
sections.mNote: The violins begin after a rest

sections.label: Var 1 · Alice’s flowing strings
sections.mNote: Oboes and bassoons sing above running violins and cellos

sections.label: Var 1 · High violins, sustained horns
sections.mNote: The violins leap upwards, marked largamente

sections.label: Coda · Strings settle in G major
sections.mNote: A final violin flourish rises into a held chord

cues.title: A rest before the phrase
cues.text: Only strings. The first violins begin after a crotchet rest, with two short notes and two longer ones; the next bar reverses their order. These small hesitations give the G-minor tune its questioning voice.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 1, opening two bars: Andante, first violins marked molto espressivo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/1e/IMSLP23792-PMLP07276-Elgar_-_Enigma_Variations_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Alice at the piano
cues.text: On 21 October 1898, after a day’s teaching, Elgar sits down at the piano. A tune catches Alice’s attention. He begins trying out versions of it as their friends might play them: the evening’s amusement becomes fourteen variations.
cues.evidence: Elgar’s account of the evening, summarised in the composition history at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enigma_Variations. The Elgar Society also recounts Alice’s response and the improvised portraits: https://elgar.org/3enigma.htm

cues.title: Alice keeps the pulse
cues.text: Caroline Alice Elgar’s portrait keeps the theme’s pace: L’istesso tempo. Oboes and bassoons sing together in G minor, while violins and cellos weave quick notes around them. The melody has company now.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, pp. 4–5, Variation I: oboes and bassoons in octaves, running first violins and divided cellos. Elgar calls the variation a prolongation of the theme in My Friends Pictured Within, section I (Novello): https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/06/IMSLP339677-SIBLEY1802.27173.6d2a-39087004945996text.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ruling the bar lines
cues.text: Alice’s support takes practical forms. She rules bar lines on Edward’s score paper and walks miles in all weathers to post manuscripts and proofs. A general’s daughter, she marries the music teacher in 1889 against her relatives’ wishes.
cues.evidence: Ian Lace, A Short Biography, Elgar Society: marriage, family opposition, score paper and journeys to post manuscripts. https://www.elgar.org/2english.htm

cues.title: Violins climb into silence
cues.text: The brass withdraws and the strings slow. In the closing bars the violins send one last run upwards. The strings settle on a G-major chord, marked ppp, under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Novello full score, p. 7, rehearsal 4 to the end of Variation I: ritardando, ascending violin figures and the final G-major chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Alice takes up the theme
transitions.how: L’istesso tempo keeps the pulse unchanged. Oboes and bassoons take up the G-minor melody together, marked largamente, over running first violins and cellos. Plucked basses support them; the second violins remain muted.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 4, the two-bar link at rehearsal 2 and the opening of Variation I.

transitions.title: The violins leap upwards
transitions.how: The second violins remove their mutes. The first violins leap into their high register, marked largamente, and descend in a long run while the horns sustain their notes. The basses return after a rest, and the timpani roll beneath the phrase.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 6: senza sordini in the second violins, largamente in the upper strings, sostenuto in the horns and a timpani roll.

transitions.title: G major, almost whispered
transitions.to: Coda · Strings settle in G major
transitions.how: The brass falls silent as the strings and woodwinds finish their phrases. Elgar marks a ritardando. A last violin run climbs above the divided violas and cellos; the basses return with the final G-major chord, held at ppp.
transitions.evidence: Novello full score, p. 7, rehearsal 4 through the final fermata of Variation I.

source.title: Elgar, Enigma Variations, full score (Novello)
source.locator: Novello full score, pp. 1–7: the opening theme and Variation I, C.A.E., through rehearsal 4.

timeline.note: First violins begin after a rest, over short notes in the second violins, violas and cellos (p. 1).
Clarinets weave around the violin melody; flutes and oboes join above sustained bassoon and horn notes (p. 2).
The violins return to the G-minor phrase, with clarinet replies and a sustained bass beneath them (p. 3).
Oboes and bassoons sing in octaves above running violins and cellos. The basses pluck their notes (p. 4).
Trombones and tuba enter quietly beneath the running violins and cellos (pp. 5–6).
The first violins leap high and descend, marked largamente. Horns sustain their notes above a timpani roll (p. 6).
Trombones and tuba finish their held notes. Woodwinds and strings carry the phrase onwards as the timpani roll subsides (p. 7).
A last violin run climbs above the divided violas and cellos. The strings settle on G major, marked ppp (p. 7).

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
